action.description: One of 'publish', 'list', 'read', 'delete', 'open', 'pin', 'unpin', 'quickstart'. Omitting it means 'publish'. **Calls** in the description says what each one does and takes, except as noted here.

file_path.description: publish: the local page Claude publishes (.html, or .md only when a skill says so). For an Artifact created from an Artifact type, it is one of that Artifact's data files. With `asset: true`, it is the local file Claude uploads. A short, distinctive basename also serves as the title when nothing else gives one.

asset.description: publish with `url`: true uploads `file_path` (or each of `file_paths`) to that artifact's asset store instead of publishing it as the page — or, with `from_url` and `asset_ids` in place of `file_path`, copies those assets of another artifact into it server side (see **Calls**).

file_paths.description: publish with `asset: true` only: several local image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in place of `file_path`, up to 25 in one call, all into the artifact that `url` names; one approval covers the call, and the result lists each file's id and url, or why it was not uploaded. A CSV, Markdown, JSON or plain-text file, a symbolic or hard link, and a file outside the working directory each go in a call of their own with `file_path`.

from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks. Ignored on an Artifact created from an Artifact type.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

edits.description: publish: small changes Claude makes to the file at `file_path` in this same call, instead of editing the file with Edit and publishing after. Use it on a page (add `url` to update an artifact from another conversation) or on one data file of an artifact made from a type (its `url`, with that file as `file_path`). Not allowed with `type_url` or `files`. Each old_str is text copied exactly from the file as it now stands and must occur in it exactly once; new_str takes its place (empty deletes it). The edits apply in order, all or none: the file is published with them and then saved with them on disk, so it stays the source for later changes; on a miss nothing is changed or published, and the result says which edit failed and why.

old_str.description: Text copied exactly from the file; must occur once.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes the published path of a `files` entry. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` is served at its path relative to `root`, unless a `files` map entry states its served path. Claude sends it with every such publish, set to the folder that holds the Artifact's files at their served paths.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

page_token.description: list only: the `next_page_token` a listing of the same scope gave, to list the artifacts after it.

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (writing people will keep editing or pass around as text, such as a memo, plan, spec, proposal or notes), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (a page to look at or use: an explainer, a diagram, anything interactive, a dashboard that shows data, anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai link (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}); a chat, project or session link is not one, and `action: "list"` lists the person's artifacts. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"). Before publishing to an artifact this conversation has neither read nor published, Claude reads it (`action: "read"`) and builds on what comes back; a publish sent without that read is refused. A refusal that hands Claude the live version counts as that read: Claude merges its changes into that version and publishes the result, and never resends the refused content unchanged. Claude omits `url` for a new artifact or to redeploy a file this conversation already published. For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

The user may see only the question dialog: tool results and text you wrote earlier in this turn may not be on their screen while it is open. Make each question stand on its own: if it depends on something you found, say so briefly, and name the items you are asking about in the question itself.

Preview feature:
Use the optional `preview` field on options when presenting concrete artifacts that users need to visually compare:
- ASCII mockups of UI layouts or components
- Code snippets showing different implementations
- Diagram variations
- Configuration examples

Preview content is rendered as markdown in a monospace box. Multi-line text with newlines is supported. When any option has a preview, the UI switches to a side-by-side layout with a vertical option list on the left and preview on the right. Do not use previews for simple preference questions where labels and descriptions suffice. Note: previews are only supported for single-select questions (not multiSelect).

questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. You will be notified when it exits — do not poll its output file while waiting. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

content.content:
# vc-x1-messages v0.3.3

Messages for the vc-x1 family. The open threads are the inbox, the history is the archive.

One shared repo every participant can reach is the only thing the protocol assumes. A thread is
one file, appended by everyone who takes part in it, so reading a conversation is reading one
file, and a search for a message's id returns everything ever said under it. Every member's
`custom.md` points at this file, and taking part means following it, pushes included.

## Terminology

Each term stands alone, a term that relies on another follows it, and a kind of a term sits
under it.

- **Member**: a participant, named by its project's name, `vc-x1`, `iiac-perf`, `zc-ring-x1`.
- **Thread**: one conversation, the file `open/m-<tid>.md` while open and `closed/m-<tid>.md`
  after, headed `# m-<tid> <title>`, each of its lines an `m-<tid>-<num>`, so `rg -w m-<tid>`
  returns the whole thread. The directory is the thread's state, and any member may write a line
  in any open thread.
- **Thread id**: `<tid>`, an integer, never reused.
  - Its store is the tracked file `threads`, one integer, the last id issued, never decreased.
  - The opener reads it, adds one, writes it back, and takes the new value, in the opening commit.
- **Title**: the opener's, a few words, never changed.
- **Line**: one message or mark, one physical line, always, appended oldest first directly
  under the heading, no blank line anywhere in the file:
  `- m-<tid>-<num> <time> from <author> <action> <info>`.
- **Number**: `<num>`, an integer from 0, one more than the last line in the file, so the thread
  is its own counter and nothing else stores it: line `<num>` is file line `<num>` plus two, and
  the next number is the file's line count less one. Every `m-<tid>-<num>` is unique and the numbers
  order the thread, so a search for one returns the line and every later line that names it. An
  id, thread or line, is final once written, since one clone mints them (see What is not here),
  and a rejected push, which only a second clone causes, renumbers before pushing again.
- **Time**: when the line was written, UTC to the second, `2026-09-09T16:05:42Z`. For a human
  reading the thread, never for ordering, as clocks may not agree.
- **Author**: the member who wrote the line, after the word `from`, which is there for the human
  eye, since the position already says it.
- **Action**: what the line does, one of two:
  - **`to`**: a message. Info is the recipients, comma-joined with no spaces, a space, then the
    text. A recipient need not have been in the thread before, so a forward is a `to` naming the
    new member and saying what is forwarded. A reply begins its text with the id it answers when
    position alone would leave that ambiguous, as in a thread of three.
  - **`done`**: a mark, no info. The author has nothing to say to the lines before it. Any line
    from a member clears what was pending for them, so this is the line for when there is
    nothing else to write, and the closer's last word.
- **Info**: the message text, or its title and a message-link to its body,
  `[<title>](m-<tid>-<num>.md)`, relative to the thread's own directory so the link survives
  the close.
- **Body**: `m-<tid>-<num>.md` beside its thread, for a message that wants more than a line. It
  begins `# m-<tid>-<num> <title>`, so a search for the id finds it and the heading is an anchor,
  and it ends at the end of the file. Full markdown inside, headings, lists, and code blocks, and
  a quoted line is inert since a body is never read for lines. Moved with its thread.
- **Addressed**: a member is addressed by every `to` line naming them in its recipient field,
  and by nothing else. A member named in a line's text or in a body is referenced, never
  addressed, so a tool computing pending reads the recipient field, not the whole line.
- **Pending**: for a member, every `to` line naming them numbered above their latest line in
  that thread, of either action, all of them when they have written none. Their open
  obligations, and what Read messages returns: a line stays pending until they write after it,
  however many times it has been read, and a later line naming them makes them pending again.
  So a reply is its author's own clearance, and a question back puts the ball in the other
  court until the answer comes.
- **Complete**: every addressed member has a line numbered above every `to` line naming them.
  Computed from the file alone.
- **Closed**: the file is under `closed/`, moved there whole with its bodies, so every thread
  ever is in the tree, in this file's shape, and a reader parses one shape. History is
  provenance, never a store. A closed thread takes no line, and a late thought opens a new
  thread naming the old id.
- **Message-link**: a live link within this repo, `[<text>](<file>#<slug>)`, relative to the
  linking file and resolving to whatever the reader's checkout holds. The form for a body.
- **Sha-link**: a URL naming a commit SHA (`blob/<sha>/<path>#<slug>`), never a branch, which
  moves or dies. The form for content in another repo, where only a commit is durable.
- **Clone**: one, on one machine, one owner at a time, since the ids are allocated under its

# Todo list

This file contains near term tasks with a short description and reference links to more details.
Its shape is [Todo format](agent-data/notes.md#todo-format).

The other files are listed in [zTOC.md](zTOC.md).

## Continuation notes

Where the agent was, for the agent that comes next. Ephemeral, never a record, read first at
acquaint, acted on, and reset to `_None._` by the reader.

- `~/tmp` holds the test workspaces of the last two cycles, disposable once nothing needs them:
  `acc/` (`a1`, `hw`, `remotes`), `t1`, `hw`, `por1`, `remotes`, `wt4` to `wt7`.
- Rung 4, **feat: a rung commits as a pair**, is committed locally as a pair, work `ptypkouvrtxx`
  and agent `rtyruusooysr`, and not pushed. `vc-x1-dev push -s b` publishes it, on wink's approval.
- The next rung, **feat: commit refuses to advance the trunk**, is planned in the ladder and its
  subsection, not started, and wink may drop it. Ask before starting. This note and those two
  entries are the work `@`'s only changes.

## In Progress

A cycle's record has one home at a time, and while the cycle runs this is it. The block's shape is
the specimen in [cycle-model.md](agent-data/cycle-model.md), and the rules are in [The In Progress
block](agent-data/notes.md#the-in-progress-block).

### chore: complete vc-x1, ready for vc-x2

#### Problem

(wink + agent, 2026-11-06) vc-x1 is to be succeeded by vc-x2, seeded from vc-x1's tree without
history, and before it is seeded vc-x1 must be complete as the archive vc-x2 refers back to. It is
not:

- 659 of its 686 work commits carry `ochid:` alone, so their agent partner is not linked by SHA
  (`ocid:`) nor their parents (`pcid:`), and 2 carry no trailer. `trailers --update` stamps all
  three, but only for a range above the trunk, and it has never been run over a whole history.
- vc-x2, starting without history, reaches the why and how of its first tree only through vc-x1's
  history, and whether `lookup` can follow it there is untested.

#### Solution

Provisional:

- `vc-x1 trailers --update --range ..@-` handles a whole history, rehearsed twice in a test repo
  made by `init --test-repo`, the code changed for the cases vc-x1's own history holds and kept for
  vc-x2 to inherit.
- The trailers name the partner by `orepo:` and `ochid:` alone, `ocid:` and `pcid:` dropped, so no
  trailer holds a SHA and a squash-push leaves both repos clean, agent-files v0.3.1-3.
- No push is forced without asking: `push` and `squash-push` ask, `--yes` answering, and `land` and
  `commit` refuse one, agent-files v0.3.1-4.
- A rung commits as a pair, `commit -s b`, so each rung's transcript is its own agent commit,
  agent-files v0.3.1-5.
- vc-x1's history is left as it is: `validate-desc` over it reports the known list,
  [vc-x1-history.md](notes/vc-x1-history.md), and nothing else. A rewrite waits on the trailer
  format vc-x2 decides, and may never be made.
- A test vc-x2 is seeded from the rehearsal without history, its first commit naming vc-x1's final
  SHA by hand, and `lookup` is tried in it. What vc-x2 needs is filed as `## Todo` entries, which
  vc-x2 inherits with `TODO.md`, not built.
- After the Land, outside the cycle: vc-x2 is seeded, a `git archive` of vc-x1's landed `main` made

repairs a dropped trailer by title match.

## Cycle bookmarks: create and land

The mechanics behind [Cycles run on a bookmark](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark). That section
holds the rule and when it applies, and this one holds the commands
([why](rationale.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land)).

**Create**, at the cycle's opening: `vc-x1 commit -s b --opening --title "<bare cycle title>" --body
"..."` commits the opening and creates the bookmark at the trunk, named by the title's slug (the
anchor algorithm in [Markdown anchor links](notes.md#markdown-anchor-links)), and kept local.

**Close**: `vc-x1 commit -s b --closing <BM|REV>`, naming the cycle's tip, makes the closing: the
merge of the trunk and the tip, or the one commit finalized in place. The trunk is `[cycle] trunk`,
`main` when absent. Without a `[closing] body` in `.vc-config.md`, it needs `--body`.

**Land**, once the close-out is approved: the sequence that makes the cycle permanent. Its `vc-x1
push` is the push under [Approval per push](../AGENTS.md#before-any-push), with the closing words
before it and silence after ([At rest](../AGENTS.md#at-rest)):

1. Sync: `vc-x1 sync -s b`, and a `main` it moved stops the Land ([Sync](../AGENTS.md#sync)).
2. Integrate: `vc-x1 land -s b --onto <trunk>`, local: it commits the agent `@` as the partner of
   the work commits that name it, none when every rung is a pair, fast-forwards the trunk, and
   deletes the cycle's local bookmark, every check made first.
   `--dry-run` says each step. The user may test here, before anything is published.
3. Publish: `vc-x1 push -s b --bookmark <trunk>`, the work repo first, the journal folded into the
   last agent commit while that is unpublished. `land --push` does steps 2 and 3 as one.
   The agent publishes only with the user's permission, and otherwise the user does after the
   session, by `vc-x1 squash-push -s b` ([At rest](../AGENTS.md#at-rest)).
4. Remote bookmark: `vc-x1 delete-bookmark -s w --bookmark <bookmark> --skip local`, when the topic
   was ever pushed.
5. Install: `vc-x1 build`, a `vc-x1 run -- -V` smoke check, and `vc-x1 install`, so the plain name
   is replaced only by what is on the trunk.

- `vc-x1 land --onto` a bookmark that is not the trunk, a stack of cycles landing together, is the
  command and not the sequence: nothing is installed, and the cycle is permanent only when it
  reaches the trunk.
- Landing is the moment the cycle's commits become permanent. No record cites their SHAs
  ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)): the landed commits are the record.
- `vc-x1 land` only fast-forwards. A trunk that moved means the closing is made again, as its merge
  has to join the new trunk.

lastPrompt: On advancing the trunk, what's the definition of a trunk, we have [cycle.trunk] defined in vc-config.md but not used/defined in .vc-config.md. But as I've said before there can be many trunks, not jus…

content.text:
You're right. Today's definition only allows one trunk per workspace, and several places don't even read that.

**What "trunk" means now**
- `vc-config.md:577` defines `cycle.trunk` as the one bookmark a closing merges onto and a bare `--land` lands on, defaulting to `main`. `.vc-config.md` doesn't set it, so it's `main`. `configured_trunk` (`src/commit.rs:1270`) reads it, and `--closing` and `trailers` use it.
- `--land <TRUNK>` can override it, but only per closing.
- Several places hardcode `main` and ignore the setting:
  - `squash`'s published-commit check: `const TRUNK = "main"` at `src/squash.rs:179`.
  - `bookmark_set("main", ...)` at `src/commit.rs:1202`.
  - `sync` defaults to `main`, and the agent-files say "a `main` it moved".
  - jj's own `trunk()` alias accepts only main, master or trunk on origin or upstream.
- I found no record of your earlier point that a release branch can be a trunk. It isn't in `TODO.md`, the backlog, or the agent-files. The rung's own text also guesses "which we think is the trunk itself", so it was written against the single-trunk idea.

**A definition that allows many trunks**
- A trunk is a long-lived, published bookmark that cycles fork from and land on, and it advances only by a Land: `main`, `release-1.x`, and so on.
- A cycle's trunk belongs to the cycle, not the workspace. It's whichever trunk the opening forks from, so `--closing` and `land` can work it out from the opening's ancestry instead of needing `--land`.
- The config turns into a set, something like `[cycle] trunks = ["main", "release-*"]`, defaulting to `["main"]`. The first entry is the default for an opening made outside any trunk's line.

**What that means for the rung**
- It becomes "commit refuses to advance any trunk": a non-opening `commit` whose nearest bookmark matches `trunks` is refused, pointing to `--opening`.
- Only `land` moves a trunk.
- Each hardcoded `main` above would read the set instead. That could go in this rung, or be filed as its own Todo.

The plain version: a trunk should mean "a bookmark cycles land on", of which there can be several, and each cycle uses the one it branched from. At the moment the code has a single setting that some commands read and others skip in favour of a hardcoded `main`.

How do you want to proceed?
- Widen this rung to the multi-trunk definition with the refusal.
- Define trunks now and file the refusal separately.
- Drop the rung for vc-x1 and file it all as a Todo for vc-x2.

lastPrompt: What if we had no notion of a trunk, just because you make a branch/bookmark doesn't mean that it is the intended target for landing, high probability but not certain.

content.text:
I think dropping the trunk works. The landing target becomes a choice made by name, and nothing has to guess it.

**What each step would do**
- **Opening:** it forks from wherever `@-` is and creates the bookmark. It already needs no trunk, it just reads one.
- **Closing:** `--closing <tip> --onto <BM>`, with the target named. The shape is counted against that target: one commit in `<BM>..<tip>` is single-step, more is a ladder, and the trapezoid's first parent is `<BM>`. A closing with no `--onto` is refused, and the message names the likely target: the bookmark on the opening's parent, which is "high probability, not certain".
- **Land:** `land --onto <BM>`, always named. That's already how `jj.md` writes it, so the "a stack lands onto a bookmark that is not the trunk" exception goes away. Landing on another cycle's bookmark is just a Land.
- **Config:** `[cycle] trunk` is removed, from both the schema and `configured_trunk`. A default the tool assumes is exactly the guess you're objecting to.

**The rung changes subject**
"Commit refuses to advance the trunk" needs a trunk. Without one, the question becomes which bookmark a plain `commit` may move. My answer would be only a cycle bookmark, meaning one whose line holds an opening titled with its own slug. Any other bookmark nearest below `@-` (`main`, a release branch, someone's long-lived line) is refused, with the error pointing to `--opening` or `--bookmark <NAME>`. That catches the accident the rung was for, recognises the cycle bookmark instead of naming a protected one, and needs no list of trunks.

**The hardcoded `main`s, each reworded**
- `squash` (`src/squash.rs:179`): "on `main`'s remote" becomes "on any remote bookmark". It's protecting published commits, so this is the more accurate check.
- `install` (`src/install_cmd.rs:65`): its report compares the binary's commit with `main` and `main@origin`. It would report the bookmarks the commit is on, or take the target from `--onto`.
- `sync`: it already takes `--bookmark`. Its default `main` would stay as a sync default, which is a different job from a landing target.
- jj's `trunk()` alias (`src/jj/session.rs:170`) is jj's notion of immutable heads, not ours. I'd leave it.

**The cost**
- Every closing and Land types `--onto <BM>`, and the agent-files lose their shorthand: "Land is onto the trunk" becomes "onto the bookmark named at the closing", and the trapezoid's "trunk line" becomes "the target's line".
- An alternative is to name the target at the opening and record it, as an `onto:` trailer stamped by `vc-x1`. I'd hold off. The target can change mid-cycle (land on the release branch after all), and the closing is where the decision is actually made.

The plain version: no trunk; you name where a cycle lands when you close it. A plain commit may only move a bookmark the tool can see is a cycle's, so nothing else gets moved by accident.

Should I rewrite the planned rung around this ("closing and land name their target, and commit moves only a cycle bookmark"), or file it as a Todo for vc-x2 and keep vc-x1's ladder as it is?

content.text:
About one rung, and mostly mechanical. Only a few places actually pick a trunk on their own; most of the 216 mentions are variable names, messages and help text.

**Code where a trunk is chosen for you**

| File | Today | Change | Size |
|---|---|---|---|
| `src/commit.rs` (66 mentions) | `--closing` uses `trunk_name`, then `configured_trunk`, then `main`. `--land [TRUNK]` has an optional value | Remove both functions. `--closing` requires `--onto <BM>`, and `--land` uses that `--onto`. About 25 test sites (16 closing, 9 land) gain `--onto main` | Medium |
| `src/trailers.rs` (17) | Default range is `trunk..@-`. It refuses a range that reaches `trunk@origin` | Require `--onto` or an explicit range. Refuse on `<onto>@origin` | Small, 2 tests |
| `src/squash.rs` (24) | `const TRUNK = "main"` makes a commit on `main@origin` need `--yes` | Either "on any remote bookmark other than the line's own" or `--onto`. This needs a design call | Small to medium |
| `src/install_cmd.rs` (26) | `const TRUNK = "main"` drives the "commit X, on `main` and `main@origin`" report | List the bookmarks that contain the commit, so no parameter is needed | Small |
| `vc-config.md`, `build.rs` | The `cycle.trunk` schema entry and `CYCLE_TRUNK_DEFAULT` | Delete both and regenerate `vc-config-model.md` | Small |

**Code that's only naming**
- `src/land.rs` (64) already has `--onto` required, so only the `trunk` names and messages change.
- `src/main.rs` (11) is help text.
- `src/merge.rs` (2) is test names.
- `src/jj/session.rs` (6) is jj's own `trunk()` alias for immutable heads. I'd leave it.

**Docs**
- In the agent-files, `AGENTS.md` (9), `jj.md` (14), `rationale.md` (4) and `versioning.md` (1) use it. "One commit above the trunk" becomes "above `--onto`", and the trapezoid's first parent becomes the target. That makes it an agent-files change, v0.3.1-6.
- `README.md` has 23 mentions.

**Adjacent, not called "trunk" but the same idea**
- `sync`'s default bookmark is `main`.
- `clone` checks that `main` is tracked.
- `commit`'s agent side sets and pushes `main` (`src/commit.rs:1202`).

These are "the repo's line" rather than a landing target. The agent-repo has no cycle bookmark, so its `main` is its only line. I'd leave these out of scope unless you want them included.

**Estimate:** one rung. I'd guess a 300–500 line diff, mostly renames and new `--onto` arguments in tests. The real decisions are:
- `--onto` required on `--closing`: every closing types it.
- What `squash` counts as published history, now that "the trunk's remote" is gone.

The plain version: two commands, `commit --closing` and `trailers`, lose a default and gain a required `--onto`. `squash` and `install` stop comparing against `main`. The rest is renaming, docs, and an agent-files version bump.

Should this replace the planned "commit refuses to advance the trunk" rung? And the plain-commit guard (moving only a cycle bookmark): in this rung, or later?

content.text:
Replacing the rung: agreed. I'll write it up once you've answered the question at the end, since your branch-first idea changes what goes in it.

**The guard: agreed, drop it**
- With `--onto` required, nothing lands anywhere you didn't name.
- One gap is left. A plain `commit` on a line with no cycle bookmark still advances the nearest bookmark locally, and that could be `main`. It only gets published by a push, and every push needs your approval, so that's the guard.
- Branch-first, below, makes the gap mostly disappear, because the nearest bookmark is the cycle's from the very first edit.

**Branch first: I think it's right**

Today the bookmark is created by `commit --opening` at the end of the opening, after the In Progress block, the ladder and the bump are already written into an un-branched `@`. Creating it first, right after the sync, means:
- Every edit of the cycle, the bump included, is on its branch from the start.
- An acquaint that finds a half-made opening sees the bookmark, so "where are we" has an answer.
- `sync --bookmark` and `status` work from the first edit.
- `commit` no longer creates bookmarks at all, so committing and branching are separate jobs.

**How I'd build it**
- Put the bookmark on `@`, the empty working copy, not on `@-`.
  - On `@-` it would sit on the same commit as `main`. The nearest-bookmark lookup then finds two and refuses, and with no trunk there's nothing to pick one by.
  - On `@` it follows the change as edits are made. When `commit` runs, `@` becomes `@-`, so the bookmark is the nearest one from then on. I'm fairly sure jj keeps a bookmark on the change through a commit, but I'll test that in the rung.
- A new command creates it, something like `vc-x1 open --title "<cycle title>"`. It refuses unless `@` is empty, then creates the title's slug as the bookmark, kept local.
- `--opening` stays on `commit`, but only for the bookend title (" opening" appended) and a check that `@-` carries a bookmark whose name is the title's slug. It no longer creates anything.
- The rules change:
  - The Opening's step 2 becomes "create the bookmark", before the In Progress block and the bump.
  - The per-rung flow gains nothing, since later rungs are already on the branch.
  - This is an agent-files change, landing in the same v0.3.1-6 as the "no trunk" text.

**One open question:** an empty `@` that gets abandoned moves its bookmark down onto `main`'s commit. That's the two-candidates case again. Either `commit` refuses with a clear message, or the bookmark is made again. I'd go with the refusal.

The plain version: create the cycle's branch first thing, on the empty working copy, with its own command. Then everything the cycle does, starting with the version bump, is on that branch, and `commit` only commits.

Should branch-first go into the same rung as "no trunk, `--onto` required", or into a rung of its own right after it? I'd make it a separate rung: the `--onto` change is mechanical, while this one changes the opening's sequence and adds a command.

content.text: Putting the bookmark on @ seems reasonable, what else will "open" do besides making a bookmark and should the parameter be --title or --bookmark, are you proposing that we make a bodyless commit?

No, I'm not proposing a commit. `open` puts a bookmark on the existing empty `@`, and the opening commit stays where it is today, made by `vc-x1 commit --opening` with its title and body.

**What `open` does**

Checks, all made before anything changes:
- The work `@` is empty, so the bookmark goes on a change that has no edits yet.
- Both repos are up to date, a `sync --dry-run` look. A repo that's behind is refused rather than synced, so the Opening's sync step stays the visible step it is now.
- The bookmark name isn't already used, either locally or on origin.

Then it does one thing: creates the bookmark on `@`, kept local. The agent-repo gets nothing, as now.

What it doesn't do: anything in `TODO.md`, `zTOC.md`, or the version. Those are the agent's edits under the Opening's steps, and keeping them out of the tool keeps it small.

**`--title`, with `--bookmark` to override**
- `--title "<bare cycle title>"` works out the bookmark name with the same slug algorithm as the `TODO.md` anchors, so the bookmark and the In Progress heading's anchor match by construction. It can also refuse a title ending in " opening" or " closing", as `--opening` already does.
- `--bookmark <NAME>` is for the rare case where you want a different name, mirroring today's `--opening [NAME]`.

**One option to consider: describe `@`, without committing**

`open` could also set `@`'s description to the opening title, "<title> opening", with no body and no trailers. It would still be the working copy, not a commit.
- **For:**
  - jj abandons an empty `@` when you move off it only if it has no description. A described one is kept, so the bookmark can't slide down onto `main`'s commit, which closes the case I raised last time.
  - `commit --opening` could then read the title from `@` and take only `--body`.
- **Against:** it's one more piece of state outside `TODO.md`. A later `commit --opening --title` that disagrees would need a rule, and I'd refuse it.
- **Rules check:** describing a fresh, never-described, local change is authoring, not the re-describe that `jj.md` forbids.

I'd include it: the protection against abandonment is worth it, and it's one jj call. I'm fairly sure about jj's auto-abandon behaviour, but the rung would test it.

The plain version: `open --title "..."` checks things are clean and in sync, then names the empty working copy as the cycle's branch, and optionally gives it the opening title so jj won't throw it away. You still make the opening commit, with its body, at the end of the opening as now.

Should `open` describe `@` with the title, or only create the bookmark?

content.text:
Agreed on the parameters: `open` takes exactly one of `--bookmark <NAME>` or `--title "<cycle title>"`, and a title is turned into the bookmark name by our slug algorithm.

**What the two `wip` commits are**

| Repo | Commit | On origin as | Content | Trailer |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| work | `sorzuwon` 55e11c19, "wip / Continue tomorrow" | the cycle bookmark `chore-complete-vc-x1-ready-for-vc-x2` | Continuation notes, plus the planned rung's subsection and ladder entry (+15 lines in `TODO.md` and `zTOC.md`) | `ochid: qxzylmupsqqw` |
| agent | `qxzylmup` c13fcf3f, "wip / Continue tomorrow" | `main`, so jj treats it as immutable | The last 16 lines of the previous session's transcript (`9dc021c3-….jsonl`) | `ochid: sorzuwonzywl` |

They form a pair: each one's `ochid:` names the other. Both are published. Neither has anything stacked on it except the two working copies, and the agent `@` holds only this session's new transcript file.

**What I suggest: remove both commits but keep their content**

1. **Work:** `jj abandon --restore-descendants sorzuwon`.
   - The commit goes away, and its 15 lines move into the work `@` as uncommitted edits.
   - The cycle bookmark moves back to rung 4 (`ptypkouv`).
   - Nothing is lost. The notes get reset at this acquaint anyway, and the planned rung's text is about to be rewritten as the `--onto` rung.
2. **Agent:** `jj abandon --restore-descendants --ignore-immutable qxzylmup`.
   - The commit goes away, and its 16 transcript lines move into the agent `@`, where the next agent commit picks them up.
   - `main` moves back to rung 4's agent commit (`rtyruusooysr`).
   - `--ignore-immutable` is needed because jj treats `main@origin` as immutable.
3. **Check:** `vc-x1 push -s b --dry-run` should show both bookmarks moving backward and nothing else.
4. **Publish:** `vc-x1 push -s b`, a forced push in both repos:
   - The cycle bookmark goes back to `6781092c`.
   - The agent `main` goes back to `2184f4ec`.

   `push` asks before a forced push. This step needs your explicit approval, and it rewinds the agent's `main` on its remote.

**Afterwards**
- Both repos are back at rung 4 and paired correctly.
- Nothing points at an abandoned change, so `validate-desc` stays clean.
- The wip content sits in the two working copies.

**Alternatives I'd skip**
- **Leave both:** the history keeps a `wip` pair, and the agent `wip` is permanent on `main`.
- **Turn the work `wip` into rung 5** by squashing into it and re-describing: the agent side's description can't be changed without the same forced push, so it saves nothing.
- **Delete the remote cycle bookmark instead of rewinding it:** that drops rung 4's only remote reference.

**One caveat:** if another clone of either repo has already fetched the `wip` commits, it will see them as divergent after the rewind. As far as I know this machine is the only one.

The plain version: undo both `wip` commits, keeping what they held as uncommitted changes, then force-push both bookmarks back one commit. Your approval is needed for that push.

If that's the plan you want, say go. I'll do steps 1–3 and stop before step 4 for your approval of the push.

content.text:
Yes, that's the same outcome as my plan: a new `@` whose parent is the commit before `wip`, holding the `wip` changes plus anything uncommitted. Then pushing `@-` moves each bookmark back. `jj abandon --restore-descendants <wip>` does exactly that in one command, and I'd use it rather than doing it by hand. Here's why:

**Doing it by hand: `jj new <before-wip>`, then `jj restore --from <wip-tree>`**
- `jj new` checks out the older tree. Any file that isn't in it is deleted from disk until the restore puts it back.
- On the agent side, that includes this session's transcript file, which Claude Code is appending to as we talk.
- It also leaves the old `wip` commits behind as stray heads that would still need abandoning.

**With `--restore-descendants`**
- `@` is re-parented onto the commit before `wip` and keeps its whole tree, so nothing on disk changes, live transcript included.
- `@`'s diff becomes the `wip` changes plus whatever was uncommitted.
- The `wip` commit is gone, and its bookmark moves down to the parent.

**Then "push `@-`"**
- Afterwards `@-` is rung 4 on each side: `6781092c` for the work repo, `2184f4ec` for the agent.
- Pushing it with each repo's bookmark (the cycle bookmark, and the agent's `main`) moves each remote back one commit. That's what `vc-x1 push -s b` does, and it's a forced push, so it asks first.

**The steps**
1. Work: `jj abandon --restore-descendants sorzuwon`.
2. Agent: `jj abandon --restore-descendants --ignore-immutable qxzylmup`.
3. `vc-x1 push -s b --dry-run`, to confirm only the two backward moves.
4. `vc-x1 push -s b`, on your separate approval.

The plain version: your idea and mine end up in the same place. The one-command version just never touches the files on disk, which matters because this conversation's transcript is one of them.

Say go and I'll do steps 1–3, then stop before the push.

Abandon a revision

Abandon a revision, rebasing descendants onto its parent(s). The behavior is similar to `jj restore
--changes-in`; the difference is that `jj abandon` gives you a new change, while `jj restore`
updates the existing change.

If a working-copy commit gets abandoned, it will be given a new, empty commit. This is true in
general; it is not specific to this command.

Usage: jj abandon [OPTIONS] [REVSETS]...

Arguments:
  [REVSETS]...
          The revision(s) to abandon (default: @) [aliases: -r]

Options:
      --retain-bookmarks
          Do not delete bookmarks pointing to the revisions to abandon
          
          Bookmarks will be moved to the parent revisions instead.

      --restore-descendants
          Do not modify the content of the children of the abandoned commits

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

Global Options:
  -R, --repository <REPOSITORY>
          Path to repository to operate on
          
          By default, Jujutsu searches for the closest .jj/ directory in an ancestor of the current
          working directory.

      --ignore-working-copy
          Don't snapshot the working copy, and don't update it
          
          By default, Jujutsu snapshots the working copy at the beginning of every command. The
          working copy is also updated at the end of the command, if the command modified the
          working-copy commit (`@`). If you want to avoid snapshotting the working copy and instead
          see a possibly stale working-copy commit, you can use `--ignore-working-copy`. This may be
          useful e.g. in a command prompt, especially if you have another process that commits the
          working copy.
          
          Loading the repository at a specific operation with `--at-operation` implies
          `--ignore-working-copy`.

      --no-integrate-operation
          Run the command as usual but don't integrate any operations
          
          When this option is given, the operations will still be created as usual but they will not
          be integrated to the operation log. The working copy will also not be updated.
          
          The command will print the resulting operation ID. You can pass that to e.g. `jj --at-op`
          to inspect the resulting repo state, or you can pass it to `jj op restore` to restore the
          repo to that state. You can also pass the ID to `jj op integrate` to integrate the
          operation.
          
          Note that this does *not* prevent side effects outside the repo. For example, `jj git push
          --no-integrate-operation` will still perform the push.

      --ignore-immutable
          Allow rewriting immutable commits
          
          By default, Jujutsu prevents rewriting commits in the configured set of immutable commits.
          This option disables that check and lets you rewrite any commit but the root commit.
          
          This option only affects the check. It does not affect the `immutable_heads()` revset or
          the `immutable` template keyword.

      --at-operation <AT_OPERATION>
          Operation to load the repo at
          
          Operation to load the repo at. By default, Jujutsu loads the repo at the most recent
          operation, or at the merge of the divergent operations if any.
          
          You can use `--at-op=<operation ID>` to see what the repo looked like at an earlier
          operation. For example `jj --at-op=<operation ID> st` will show you what `jj st` would
          have shown you when the given operation had just finished. `--at-op=@` is pretty much the
          same as the default except that divergent operations will never be merged.
          
          Use `jj op log` to find the operation ID you want. Any unambiguous prefix of the operation
          ID is enough.
          
          When loading the repo at an earlier operation, the working copy will be ignored, as if
          `--ignore-working-copy` had been specified.
          
          It is possible to run mutating commands when loading the repo at an earlier operation.
          Doing that is equivalent to having run concurrent commands starting at the earlier
          operation. There's rarely a reason to do that, but it is possible.
          
          [alias: --at-op]

      --debug
          Enable debug logging

      --color <WHEN>
          When to colorize output
          
          [possible values: always, never, debug, auto]

      --quiet
          Silence non-primary command output
          
          For example, `jj file list` will still list files, but it won't tell you if the working
          copy was snapshotted or if descendants were rebased.
          
          Warnings and errors will still be printed.

      --no-pager
          Disable the pager

      --config <NAME=VALUE>
          Additional configuration options (can be repeated)
          
          The name should be specified as TOML dotted keys. The value should be specified as a TOML

content.text:
You're right to ask. A plain `jj abandon` does revert, which we don't want. I also had the bookmark behaviour wrong. I ran all three variants in throwaway repos (`/tmp/claude-1000/-home-wink-data-prgs-rust-vc-x1/4ae2c927-6ac1-4b89-b073-02c4913ee2e1/scratchpad/abandon-demo.sh`). Each starts with `rung4`, then `wip` carrying the `topic` bookmark, then `@` holding an uncommitted `session.txt`.

| Command | `wip`'s changes | `topic` bookmark | Files on disk |
|---|---|---|---|
| `jj abandon wip` | **Gone**: removed from `@` and from disk, a revert | **Deleted** | `wip.txt` deleted, `a.txt` rolled back |
| `jj abandon --restore-descendants wip` | Kept, now `@`'s diff | **Deleted** | Unchanged |
| `jj abandon --restore-descendants --retain-bookmarks wip` | Kept, now `@`'s diff | **Moved to `rung4`** | Unchanged |

- `--restore-descendants` is what stops the revert. The help puts it as "do not modify the content of the children": `@` keeps its exact tree, so its diff grows to include `wip`'s changes.
- Without `--retain-bookmarks`, jj deletes the bookmark. Earlier I said it moves to the parent; it doesn't, unless you ask for it. Without the flag we'd have lost the local cycle bookmark and the agent's local `main`.

**The corrected commands**
1. Work: `jj abandon --restore-descendants --retain-bookmarks sorzuwon`
2. Agent: `jj -R .agent-session abandon --restore-descendants --retain-bookmarks --ignore-immutable qxzylmup`
3. `vc-x1 push -s b --dry-run`, which should show only the two bookmarks moving back one commit.
4. `vc-x1 push -s b`, the forced push, on your approval.

The plain version: plain abandon throws the changes away. With both flags it removes only the commit: the changes stay in your working copy and the bookmark steps back one commit, which is the "branch off the commit before and carry everything forward" you described.

Go for steps 1–3?

content.text:
No, `restore` isn't what we need here. `restore` copies file contents into a commit; it doesn't remove a commit from the graph. What we want is the `wip` commit gone, with its content carried forward, and that's `abandon`'s job.

- **What `restore` would do:** `jj restore --from ptypkouv --into sorzuwon` makes `wip`'s files match rung 4's. `wip` is emptied, but it's still there, still described "wip", and still carrying the bookmark. On its own it also changes `@`'s content, the revert again, unless descendants are protected. We'd then have to abandon the empty `wip` anyway, so it's two steps to reach what one `abandon` does.
- **What `abandon --restore-descendants --retain-bookmarks` does:** removes the `wip` commit, re-parents `@` onto rung 4 with `@`'s tree untouched, and moves the bookmark to rung 4. The demo showed exactly that.
- The help you pasted says the same: plain `restore` "is similar to `jj abandon`, except that it leaves an empty revision with its description". Keeping the empty "wip" commit is what we're trying to avoid.

The plain version: `restore` edits what's inside a commit, and `abandon` removes the commit. We want the commit gone and its content kept, so abandon with both flags.

content.content:
vc-x1 0.85.20+ffa3ba138597

Publish a rung's pair: the work commit on its bookmark and the
agent commit on `main`. Push carries no description and writes
none, so what was reviewed is what goes out.

`commit` makes the pair, both commits now (-s b) or the work
half with its trailer naming the agent @ (-s w). Push publishes
the work @-, so new work in @ is left as it is, and it refuses
a work @- with no `ochid:` trailer, which is not a pair's commit.

The halves are independent, each trailer being fixed before
push runs, so -s b is -s a then -s w, the order the pair is
completed in:
  - agent  complete the partner by the state found: fold the
           journal into a committed one, or commit it as the
           partner when pending or the agent repo changed;
           then squash-push main
  - work   restamp the unpublished work commit if its trailer
           does not name the partner, then set and push
           <bookmark>

-s is required: `b` both halves, `a` the agent half, `w` the work
half, `p` a plain repo's @- on its bookmark. -R is optional and
says where. --bookmark is the line's unless named, as a check or
as a new name created at @- and pushed tracked.

-r names another commit, already made, and a name alone goes out
for it, no pair: the one bookmark at it, or --bookmark's, that
bookmark or a new one created there. The working copy and the
root are refused, and so is a REV of several commits.

Every argument is a flag: the old positional is refused, naming
--bookmark or -r, the one it was.

Rerunning is always safe: a half whose work is done finds nothing
to do. A half that fails before its own push restores the repo it
touched via `jj op restore`.

Usage: vc-x1 push [OPTIONS] --scope <SCOPE>

Options:
  -r, --revision <REV>
          The commit to publish, one: `@-` publishes the pair, any other a name
          alone [default: `@-`]

  -V, --version...
          Version detail on stdout: -V the banner, -VV the full report (as
          `vc-x1 version`). Counted like -v/-vv.
          
          Both ride along: they print, then the subcommand runs, so one
          invocation captures the version and the command's output together.
          That is why this replaces clap's auto-version, which would exit after
          printing. Without either, the banner still prints, on stderr.

      --bookmark <NAME>
          The remote's name for it: a bookmark on the line, moved there, one
          already at REV, or a new name, created there [default: the line's
          bookmark, or the one at REV]

      --no-banner
          Suppress the banner stderr normally carries on every run.
          
          Only the ambient banner: an explicit `-V` still prints, since asking
          for it outranks suppressing it.

      --allow-jj-mismatch
          Run even when `jj -V` disagrees with our linked jj-lib.
          
          Per-invocation on purpose, never a config key: a key gets set once
          during a frustrating afternoon and then silently protects nothing.

  -R, --repo <PATH>
          Where: a path in the workspace for `-s b|w|a`, its root or either
          repo, or the repo itself for `-s p` [default: the current directory]

  -s, --scope <SCOPE>
          Which repos, required: `w|work`, `a|agent`, `b|both`, or `p|por`
          
          [possible values: work, agent, both, por]

  -v, --verbose...
          Verbose output: -v debug, -vv trace

      --log <LOG>
          Log file path (captures all levels)

      --step
          Pause between every stage for an interactive approval gate

      --dry-run
          Print the exact commands for every stage without side effects

  -y, --yes
          Pass the `--step` gates without asking

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
