tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

content.text:
Yes, there's a difference. `--onto` names the target, and `--land` moves it.

**Without `--land`** (`commit --closing @- --onto main --push ...`):
- The closing is made. In your case that's `@` committed as the cycle's one commit. `--onto main` is what it's checked against: the branch must descend from `main`, and here that means one commit above it. For a ladder, `main` is also the merge's first parent.
- `main` doesn't move.
- `single-step-abc` stays on the closing.
- `--push` publishes `single-step-abc` to origin as a draft branch, not `main`.
- The Land is still to come, as a separate step: `vc-x1 land -s b --source single-step-abc --onto main --push`.

**With `--land`**, the same invocation also runs that Land:
- It commits the agent `@` and updates the trailers.
- It fast-forwards `main` to the closing and deletes `single-step-abc`.
- With `--push`, it publishes `main` in both repos and deletes the bookmark on origin.

**Why it's opt-in:** the protocol treats these as two moments. The closing is the agent's to make, at close-out step 5. The Land is step 7, "on the user's go". The gap between them is where you review the finished closing before `main` becomes permanent. If `--onto` implied `--land`, closing without landing would need a `--no-land` flag, and the default would skip that stop. Landing is also the less reversible of the two: once `main` is pushed, the cycle is published.

**My recommendation:** keep `--land` opt-in. This is also the open question I raised earlier: whether `commit --land` should exist at all. With `vc-x1 land` there, the one-shot form only saves typing. The vc-x2 `cycle close` / `cycle land` split would make those two moments explicit. I'd add "drop `commit --land`" to that Todo rather than change it in this rung, if you agree.

The plain version: `--onto main` says where the cycle is going, and `--land` actually puts it there. Without `--land` you get a finished closing on its branch, and `main` waits for a separate `vc-x1 land`.

content.text:
Yes, that's correct. In each repo, `vc-x1 commit --title ".." --body ".." -s b` does what `jj commit` does:

- **Work-repo:** `@` is described with the title and body and becomes `@-`. A new empty `@` is made on top of it.
- **Agent-repo:** the same happens, as the pair's other half. The two commits are linked by their `ochid:` trailers.
- **Bookmark:** the bookmark on the line moves to the new `@-`. On a branch made by `open`, that's the cycle's bookmark. `--no-advance` leaves it where it is, and `--bookmark <NAME>` picks one when there are several.
- **Nothing is pushed** unless you add `--push`.

That plain form is every commit of a cycle except the last. `--onto` only appears with `--closing`, because that's the one commit that needs to know the target:

- **Ladder:** the closing commit is a merge of the target and the ladder's tip. `--onto` names the merge's first parent.
- **Single-step (your case):** nothing is merged. `--onto` is only used to check that the branch sits one commit above `main`, and it tells `--land` where to land.

So in the single-step case, `--onto` does almost nothing unless you also pass `--land`. That may be the confusing part.

The plain version: a plain commit does exactly what you described. `--onto` only matters for the last commit, and in a single-step cycle it's little more than a check unless you also land.

##### feat: open makes the cycle's bookmark first

The cycle's bookmark is made by `commit --opening`, after the opening's record, ladder, and bump
are already written on no branch. `vc-x1 open --title "<cycle title>"`, or `--bookmark <NAME>`,
makes it first, on `@`, the title made a name by the anchor algorithm, which is the reason for a
command over `jj bookmark create`. Agent-files v0.3.1-7.

* `open` refuses only what is dangerous, wink's: a name in use locally or on `origin`, which it
  would move. `@` may hold edits, which become the opening's, and a repo not up to date with its
  remote is a warning, a Land onto a target that moved being refused anyway. `--dry-run` prints
  the name. The agent-repo gets no bookmark.
* `open` only makes the bookmark, `@` undescribed: jj keeps an empty `@` that carries a bookmark
  when it is left, described or not, and the bookmark stays with the change through a commit, a
  test of 2026-11-10, so a description would protect nothing.
* `commit --opening` creates nothing: it gives the bookend title and refuses an `@` without the
  bookmark, the one named or the title's slug, naming `vc-x1 open --bookmark <NAME>`. Its `--skip`,
  now `--land`'s alone, and the publishing of the name alone go, the bookmark never standing apart
  from the opening, `--no-advance` with it is refused, having nothing to move, and `--opening
  --push` is a rung's push. The tests open a cycle as `open` does, the bookmark on `@` first.
* A branch with nothing committed above the target, its work in `@` on `open`'s bookmark, closes in
  one commit made from `@`, wink's (2026-11-10): the single-step flow `open` makes, open, edit,
  close, which had refused "nothing above 'main' to close". `--title` and `--body` are required,
  there being no opening to read, the tip is `@-`, the bookmark, or `@`, and the closing's bookmark
  and Land are planned from the state after the commit. An empty `@`, no bookmark on it, and
  `--dead-end` are refused, and so is `@` as the tip of a branch with commits.
* `--land <value>`, the form before rung 5, was read as the retired positional and refused naming
  `-r`, so it is refused naming `--onto <value> --land`, `--land` taking no value, the target
  needing a flag of its own for a closing that does not land, wink's.
* The Opening's step 2 runs `vc-x1 open`, before the In Progress block and the bump. It resolves
  the Todo **Every cycle commits its opening first**, a cycle with no bookmark until its opening's
  review, so that entry goes.
* Named `open` as `land` is, a cycle's verbs needing no noun, wink's. A `cycle` command is
  **vc-x2: a cycle command, open, close, and land**.

##### chore: a test vc-x2 reaches vc-x1's history

Whether vc-x2, seeded without history, can reach the why and how of its first tree in vc-x1 is
untested. A test vc-x2 is seeded from the rehearsal, its first commit naming vc-x1's final SHA, and
`lookup` is tried in it. What vc-x2 needs is filed as `## Todo` entries: a `seeded-from:` trailer
and `lookup` following it, adopt taking a renamed config, an agent across several work-repos, the
push-time check, and the xtask move.

##### chore: complete vc-x1, ready for vc-x2 closing

Closing out the cycle.

## Waiting

Important work that cannot start yet. Each entry names what it waits on, in a form that can be
checked, and the rank it takes in `## Todo` once unblocked. Every opening checks each condition
and promotes what is met ([Opening](AGENTS.md#opening)).

- **Retire the frozen history: `notes/chores/` and `notes/done.md`.** (wink, 2026-08-27) They
  are frozen and no longer grow, and the agent-repo transcript plus git history hold what they
  hold. Delete both in one cycle, after a sweep turns every link into them (Todo entries, the
  backlog, rationale.md, the other members' messages) into a permalink at the SHA before the
  deletion.
  - Waits on: **`vc-x1 closed "<title>"`** landed, and the session viewer good enough to read
    a cycle's record from the transcript.
  - Place when unblocked: first.
- **Sync's remote look stops spawning git.** (wink + agent, 2026-10-09) Sync learns where a
  remote's bookmarks are by spawning `git ls-remote`, and downloads the commits of the ones that
  moved by spawning a `git fetch` that moves no ref, the sixth entry of the spawn register in
  `clippy.toml` and the one spawn of `git`. Replace `git_command` and its two callers in
  `src/jj/session.rs` with jj-lib's query, delete the `#[allow]`, and close the entry.

Yes, moving the bookmark is intended. In your second run, `single-step-2` was on `@-`, the nearest bookmark on the line, so the commit moved it to the new commit. That's working as designed.

Your first run was still a real bug. There, `single-step-abc` was on `@` itself, which is the nearest bookmark. The old code started looking at `@-`, so it skipped `single-step-abc` and moved `main` instead. With the fix, a plain commit moves the bookmark like this:

- **A bookmark on `@`** (what `open` makes): it stays with the commit, and nothing else moves.
- **No bookmark on `@`**: the nearest bookmark below is moved to the new commit, which is your second run.
- **Several bookmarks equally near**: the commit is refused. `--bookmark <NAME>` picks one.
- **`--no-advance`**: nothing moves.

One thing to keep in mind: if you commit with no branch, so `main` is the nearest bookmark, the commit moves `main`. That's why the protocol runs `open` first. `--no-advance` stops it when you don't want it.

Both runs report the same version string, `0.85.21-6+516292b4a960.dirty`, so I can't tell which build made your second run. Either build gives the same result there, since no bookmark was on `@`.

content.text:
I agree with the principle. The question is where the "asking" happens, because something has to move the cycle's bookmark.

**Why it moves at all:** a bookmark points at one commit. `open` puts it on `@`, and jj carries it along when that change is committed, so the first commit is covered. After that the bookmark sits on `@-`. When the next rung is committed, nothing moves the bookmark, so it stays one commit behind the tip. Each further rung leaves it further behind. Three things depend on it being at the tip:

- `push`, which publishes the bookmark
- `--closing <bookmark>`, which names the tip
- `land`

So without some kind of advance, every rung would need a manual `jj bookmark set`. The auto-advance exists to save that step, the way git does with a checked-out branch.

**What's wrong with it now:** it guesses. "The nearest bookmark on the line" is a heuristic, and a heuristic will sometimes pick `main`, as it just did. Refusing when the choice is ambiguous helps, but it doesn't catch one wrong nearest bookmark.

**Options, in the order I'd rank them:**

1. **`open` is the ask.** `open` records which bookmark is the cycle's, and `commit` advances that one and no other. If nothing is recorded, nothing moves, and `commit` says so ("no bookmark moved, `--bookmark <NAME>` moves one"). jj has no per-bookmark metadata, so the record would need a home: jj's repo config, a file in `.jj/`, or the cycle record. This fits "only when asked": you ask once, at `open`, not on every commit.
2. **Explicit every time:** `--bookmark <NAME>` on each commit, and no advance without it. This is the purest version of the principle, but the protocol's per-rung commit would carry the name every time. It's easy to forget, and forgetting leaves the bookmark behind silently.
3. **A guard on the heuristic:** keep the nearest-bookmark rule, but never auto-advance an immutable bookmark (jj's `immutable()`, the concept rung 5 adopted). That would have protected `main` once it tracks origin. It's still a guess, though, and a bookmark that isn't pushed yet, like your local `main*`, isn't immutable, so it might not have caught your case.

I'd go with option 1. It also matches the vc-x2 `cycle` command Todo, where `cycle open` naturally knows its bookmark and `cycle close` and `cycle land` use it. For vc-x1 I'd either file this under that Todo, or make it a rung of its own after this one, rather than widening rung 6. Rung 6's fix (checking `@` first) still stands either way: it's the right behaviour for whatever guessing remains.

The plain version: the bookmark has to move as the branch grows, or push and land point at the wrong commit. The problem is that commit guesses which bookmark. I'd have `open` say which bookmark the cycle uses and have commit move only that one, and nothing otherwise.

### chore: complete vc-x1, ready for vc-x2

#### Problem

(wink + agent, 2026-11-06) vc-x1 is to be succeeded by vc-x2, seeded from vc-x1's tree without
history, and before it is seeded vc-x1 must be complete as the archive vc-x2 refers back to. It is
not:

- 659 of its 686 work commits carry `ochid:` alone, so their agent partner is not linked by SHA
  (`ocid:`) nor their parents (`pcid:`), and 2 carry no trailer. `trailers --update` stamps all
  three, but only for a range above the trunk, and it has never been run over a whole history.
- vc-x2, starting without history, reaches the why and how of its first tree only through vc-x1's
  history, and whether `lookup` can follow it there is untested.

#### Solution

Provisional:

- `vc-x1 trailers --update --range ..@-` handles a whole history, rehearsed twice in a test repo
  made by `init --test-repo`, the code changed for the cases vc-x1's own history holds and kept for
  vc-x2 to inherit.
- The trailers name the partner by `orepo:` and `ochid:` alone, `ocid:` and `pcid:` dropped, so no
  trailer holds a SHA and a squash-push leaves both repos clean, agent-files v0.3.1-3.
- No push is forced without asking: `push` and `squash-push` ask, `--yes` answering, and `land` and
  `commit` refuse one, agent-files v0.3.1-4.
- A rung commits as a pair, `commit -s b`, so each rung's transcript is its own agent commit,
  agent-files v0.3.1-5.
- No trunk: every target is named, `commit --closing` and `trailers` taking a required `--onto`,
  and `[cycle] trunk` removed.
- Branch first: `vc-x1 open` makes the cycle's bookmark on the work `@` before the opening's first
  edit, and `commit --opening` creates nothing.
- vc-x1's history is left as it is: `validate-desc` over it reports the known list,
  [vc-x1-history.md](notes/vc-x1-history.md), and nothing else. A rewrite waits on the trailer
  format vc-x2 decides, and may never be made.
- A test vc-x2 is seeded from the rehearsal without history, its first commit naming vc-x1's final
  SHA by hand, and `lookup` is tried in it. What vc-x2 needs is filed as `## Todo` entries, which
  vc-x2 inherits with `TODO.md`, not built.
- After the Land, outside the cycle: vc-x2 is seeded, a `git archive` of vc-x1's landed `main` made
  the new root of `winksaville/vc-x2`, with a fresh `vc-x2.agent-session`, both adopted. A
  continuation note in vc-x2's `TODO.md`, committed after the seed, hands the work to vc-x2's own
  session, each push with wink's approval. Whether vc-x1's final `main` is tagged is wink's call.

#### Acceptance check

Provisional:

- In a fresh clone of the real remotes, `vc-x1 validate-desc` over each side reports an `err` or a
  `miss` for the known list's commits and for no others.
- The dry run over `..@-` sorts every commit into rewritten, already current, or left with its
  reason, and none is left unexplained.
- In the test vc-x2, `lookup` reaches vc-x1's history for a sample of lines, by the hand-written
  link if need be, and what vc-x2 must build to do it properly is a Todo entry.

#### Deliberation

- Retitled, wink's (2026-11-06): the cycle opened as **make vc-x1 content agnostic**, from the Todo
  **Build config moves to an xtask**, and the deliberation moved that subject to vc-x2, leaving
  this cycle the completing of vc-x1. The Todo returned to `## Todo` unchanged.
- vc-x2 is seeded from vc-x1, wink's (2026-11-06): content agnostic, and its design is vc-x2's, not
- **deliberation**: how the other five were decided, one bullet per decision. The bullet's lead
  names the decision and its sentence states it, and the sub-bullets carry the reasons, the
  alternatives weighed, and the costs accepted, so a reader can skim the decisions and read the
  reasons only where they doubt one. `_None._` when there was nothing to deliberate, which is a real
  answer
- **rungs**: a `#### Rungs` heading over the rung subsections, the ladder itself being `zTOC.md`'s
  ([zTOC format](#ztoc-format)): one rung per step, `- 2 (done) [<title>](TODO.md#<slug>)`: the
  rung's version suffix, which `-V` and the installed dev build print, then the marker, `(done)` or
  `(current)`, both first so they read down their columns, and a rung not yet started has neither,
  its suffix being set when its commit bumps the version, and an inline link so the ladder is one
  list with nothing beside it to keep in step, its line as long as the title makes it. `<title>` is
  the rung's commit title, `<type>: <desc>` per [Conventional-commit
  shape](prose.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit), so a moved `## Todo` entry is retitled.
  The closing rung, `<cycle title> closing`, is linked like the rest

`#### Rungs` holds the **rung subsections**, one per rung in the ladder's order, the closing
included, headed by the rung's exact title, so the ladder is their index. Each opens at laddering
with an abstract-sized intent statement (the rung's problem and solution in a sentence or two) and
completes at the rung's landing with the conceptual delta: design points, consequences, deferrals,
never a restatement of the landed commit body. The closing rung's opens with the stub "Closing out
the cycle." and completes at close-out with what closing taught, in problem/solution form, or
`_None._`.

A rung is `- N (marker) [<title>](TODO.md#<slug>)` and carries no detail beyond that: the title
links to the rung's subsection. A step is identified by its title (prose.md's [Steps are named, not
numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)), so a title carries no number, no version, and no
SHA. The version-of-record still bumps for every rung and its suffix still encodes the stage, but
that encoding belongs to the manifest and appears nowhere in prose.

A single-step cycle's ladder is one unlinked rung, `- N (marker) <cycle title>`, with no subsection
under it: a subsection headed by the title would collide with the title heading's anchor ([Cycle
shape](../AGENTS.md#cycle-shape)).

The block is the cycle's only record. A design finding that must outlive the cycle goes into a
`notes/` file by the rung that made it ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)).
